nameStory: The flea jumping spider earned its common name from its tiny size and incredible jumping ability, much like the fleas that plague our pets. When startled, this minuscule spider can leap many times its own body length in a single bound, disappearing from view in an instant just like a flea would.
description: The flea jumping spider is one of New England's tiniest jumping spiders, typically measuring just 2-4 millimeters in length. These compact spiders have the characteristic stocky build and large front-facing eyes of all jumping spiders, but in a remarkably small package. Their bodies are usually dark brown to black with subtle markings, and despite their diminutive size, they're active hunters that stalk prey rather than building webs.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small at just 2-4mm long - about the size of a large aphid or small ant, easily overlooked without close inspection

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large front-facing eyes arranged in a square pattern, giving them an alert, almost curious expression when viewed head-on

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and stocky with a slightly flattened appearance, proportionally wider than many other jumping spiders

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions and can make impressive leaps when disturbed, often seeming to vanish instantly

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Dark brown to black coloration with subtle lighter markings that may be difficult to see without magnification

habitat: Look for flea jumping spiders on tree bark, fence posts, and wooden structures where they hunt for tiny prey like springtails and aphids. They're particularly common on sun-warmed surfaces of oak, maple, and pine trees, often found scurrying along the textured bark in search of food. You might also spot them on outdoor furniture, deck railings, and the sides of buildings.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, often seen sunning themselves on tree bark and wooden surfaces during mild afternoons.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible hunting during daylight hours. Mating displays and egg-laying occur during this time.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, with spiders focusing on feeding before winter. Young spiders from summer eggs may be observed.
seasonality.winter: Adults and juveniles overwinter under loose bark, in crevices, and other protected spots, remaining inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Despite being smaller than many ants, flea jumping spiders can leap up to 20 times their own body length - equivalent to a human jumping over a 10-story building in a single bound!
confusionNotes: Most commonly mistaken for tiny ants or other small insects due to their size. Look for the jumping spider's characteristic eye arrangement and stocky build - ants have narrow waists and different eye placement, plus they move in steady lines rather than the jerky, stop-and-go motion of jumping spiders.
compareHints: Flea jumping spiders are significantly smaller than most other jumping spiders in New England, making size the easiest distinguishing feature. While bold jumping spiders and zebra jumping spiders can reach 10-15mm, the flea jumping spider maxes out at just 4mm. They also lack the bold patterns and bright colors of many other jumping spider species, instead sporting more subdued earth tones.
